t: Coral reefs are recovering. The Great Barrier Reef has record coral cover.
x: Coral cover did reach record highs on parts of the Great Barrier Reef in 2022–24, mostly fast-growing corals that also die fastest. Then the 2024 mass bleaching brought the largest one-year drops on record. The evidence Australia's marine institute (AIMS) found that from 2024 to 2025, coral cover fell from 39.8% to 30% in the northern reef, from 33.2% to 28.6% in the central reef and from 38.9% to 26.9% in the southern reef. The main cause was heat stress from the 2024 mass bleaching, helped by cyclones and crown-of-thorns starfish. Mass bleaching events now come every few years instead of once in decades. The fast-growing table corals that drive the quick recoveries are also the most easily killed by heat and storms, so the reef swings up and down more. Warm-water reefs are among the systems most at risk: the IPCC expects 70–90% of them to decline at 1.5 °C, and more than 99% at 2 °C. t: Ocean acidification is a myth. The sea is alkaline.
x: The sea is alkaline, and it is becoming less so. "Acidification" describes the direction of change, the way "cooling" describes coffee that is still hot. The evidence The ocean takes up about a quarter of the CO₂ we emit. Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, so the pH falls. Surface pH has dropped by about 0.1 since pre-industrial times. pH is logarithmic, so that means about 30% more hydrogen ions. It is measured directly, for example near Hawaiʻi since 1988. See the data Shell-building animals, such as oysters, mussels, some plankton and corals, need carbonate ions, which become scarcer as the pH falls. Oyster hatcheries in the US Pacific Northwest have already had to treat their water. This is the one effect of CO₂ that has nothing to do with temperature, so arguments about warming don't touch it. t: We'll just adapt, like the Dutch did.

The evidence The Netherlands spends over a billion euros a year on its Delta Programme, with centuries of experience and one of the world's richest economies. Most low-lying countries have neither. The IPCC finds that some hard limits to adaptation have already been reached, for some coral reefs, coastal wetlands, and polar and mountain ecosystems, and soft limits for some small farmers and coastal communities. More limits come with each extra fraction of a degree. Sea walls don't help against heat waves, crop failures or water shortages. Each needs its own, separate adaptation. Adaptation buys time; the size of the job depends on how much more warming there is. See also "only least-cost measures" . Sources: IPCC AR6 Working Group II, Summary for Policymakers ; Dutch Delta Programme “Nothing can be done” And finally: it's too late, someone else should go first, or the fixes don't work.

t: It's too late, so nothing we do matters anymore.
x: Some of it is too late, and no one can promise how this ends. But the physics is clear that what we do still sets how much worse it gets, and whatever warming we lock in lasts for thousands of years. That is a reason to keep going, not to stop. What is already too late Over the last 12 months the planet was about … warmer than before industrialization. The UN now accepts that passing the Paris limit of 1.5 °C can no longer be avoided. See the data Sea level will keep rising for centuries, and many coral reefs are probably lost. Getting back to the climate of the 20th century would take thousands of years, unless CO₂ is removed from the air on a huge scale. What is still open Warming roughly stops once CO₂ emissions reach net zero. The ocean would keep taking up heat, but the oceans and forests would also keep absorbing CO₂, and the two effects roughly cancel. So the temperature we end up with is close to the temperature on the day we reach net zero. One complication: burning coal and oil also releases aerosols, tiny particles that reflect sunlight and cool the planet. As fossil fuels are cut, that cooling disappears too, and some hidden warming comes out. James Hansen, Leon Simons and colleagues argue this effect is larger than most estimates and is already speeding up warming; many other scientists think it is smaller. Even their paper finds that phasing out emissions quickly would prevent most of the long-term warming. See the energy imbalance That day is not set by physics

t: Renewables can't run a modern grid. The wind doesn't always blow.

The wind is rarely calm everywhere at once, so linking regions smooths the supply. Batteries cover hours; hydro, pumped storage and other flexible plants cover longer gaps. Battery storage is being built very fast and has become much cheaper; it now keeps grids stable in places like California and Texas through the evening peak. t: Electric cars are worse than petrol cars, because of the batteries and mining.
x: Making an electric car does cause more emissions, mostly from the battery. Over a car's life, a battery electric car in Europe causes roughly 60–70% less greenhouse gas than a petrol car; in the US, China and India it is also much lower (ICCT 2021). As electricity gets cleaner, electric cars get cleaner too, during the car's life. Mining for batteries has real environmental and human costs that need better rules. But a petrol car burns about its own weight in fuel every year or two, and that fuel is mined and drilled too, and burned only once. Battery materials can be recycled; burned petrol can't. t: Solar panels take more energy to make than they ever produce.

t: Wind turbines kill birds.
x: They do, and that should be kept as low as possible. But turbines kill far fewer birds than cats, windows or cars, and simple fixes help: painting one blade black cut bird deaths by about 70% in a Norwegian study. Climate change threatens far more birds. The evidence In the US, cats kill an estimated 1.3–4 billion birds a year and collisions with buildings up to about a billion. Wind turbines kill a few hundred thousand. Siting matters most: keeping turbines out of migration routes and away from cliffs where birds of prey hunt. At the Smøla wind farm in Norway, painting one of the three blades black made it easier for birds to see the rotor, and deaths fell by about 72% (May et al. 2020). Pausing turbines when large flocks pass also works. Climate change puts about two-thirds of North American bird species at risk of extinction if warming continues (Audubon). t: Technology will fix it later: carbon capture, or geoengineering.
x: Some CO₂ removal will be needed. But today it removes a tiny fraction of what we emit, at a high price. Not emitting a metric ton is far cheaper than taking it back out of the air. The evidence Almost all CO₂ removal today is trees and soils. New methods, including machines that pull CO₂ from the air, remove around a million metric tons a year, against about 40 billion metric tons emitted, and machine capture costs several hundred dollars a metric ton (State of Carbon Dioxide Removal). Every metric ton left in the air keeps warming for centuries. Waiting for a future fix means that fix has to remove all the extra CO₂ too. Blocking sunlight (geoengineering) wouldn't stop ocean acidification, and stopping it suddenly would bring the delayed warming back within a few years. The tools that cut emissions the most are cheap and available now: solar, wind, efficiency, electric heat and transport (IPCC). See "only least-cost measures" . t: Individual action is pointless. BP invented the carbon footprint.
x: Both are partly true: BP did popularize the personal "carbon footprint", and the biggest cuts come from changing energy systems, not from guilt. The evidence BP's advertising campaign in the mid-2000s made the personal carbon footprint famous, shifting attention from producers to consumers. Systems matter most: how electricity is made, how cities are built, what cars and heating are on sale. Those change through policy, investment and votes. Choices still count, especially the big ones: how we heat and cool our homes, what we drive, how often we fly, what we eat. In rich countries they can cut a household's emissions substantially. Early buyers of solar panels, heat pumps and electric cars helped make them cheap for everyone. And what people buy, say and vote for tells companies and politicians what is wanted. t: Water vapor tracker
x: How much water vapor the atmosphere holds, month by month since 1940, and how it rises with temperature. Copernicus ERA5. 1 kg/m² of water vapor is a 1 mm layer of water if it all fell as rain at once. The whole atmosphere holds about 25 mm, some 13,000 km³: if it all rained out, it would fill Lake Erie about 26 times. The air recycles that water every 10 days or so. How much water vapor the air holds, averaged over the whole globe. Warmer air holds more: about 7% more for every 1 °C (basic physics). More water in the air means heavier downpours, and, with rain coming in bigger bursts, longer dry spells in between (IPCC). A downpour does not make up for a dry spell: rain that falls faster than the soil can soak it up runs off, causing floods, instead of reaching the roots and groundwater.
